Messages.Author: L. Scott Johnson
Messages.Body:
OK Design Team: I can't use reaction cards to respond to a Malk who
takes an action on my turn because the rules state:
"These cards can only be played when it is not your turn."

Fine. Stick your collective head in the sand and ignore the fact that
you failed to consider this card when writing the rules.

But, the Malk taking the action cannot use any action cards, right:
7.2.2:
"your minions may only use action cards on your turn."

So, the Malk can bleed me, hunt, or take an action allowed by a card
in play. *Nothing Else*.

Now, are you going to continue to stonewall this one or are you going to
issue the long-awaited errata that:
Reaction cards may be used in response to another Methuselah's Minion's
action, even if taken on your own turn.

Well?

P.S. I don't really expect a response, of course. But I feel better
anyhow.

Messages.Author: Stephen Beaulieu
Messages.Body:
In article <3lrlhc$g...@redwood.cs.scarolina.edu>,

> OK Design Team: I can't use reaction cards to respond to a Malk who
> takes an action on my turn because the rules state:
> "These cards can only be played when it is not your turn."
> Fine. Stick your collective head in the sand and ignore the fact that
> you failed to consider this card when writing the rules.

> Now, are you going to continue to stonewall this one or are you going to
> issue the long-awaited errata that:
> Reaction cards may be used in response to another Methuselah's Minion's
> action, even if taken on your own turn.

Hear, Hear! I second the outburst from the Honorable Elder!

The real difficulty with writing rules for a game like Jyhad lies in the
fact that a generic rule gets overridden by the text on the cards. Of
course, this is what makes a CCG like Jyhad so much fun to play. It is
virtually infinitely expandable. The problem is that if you word the
generic rules too genericly (reaction only when it's not your turn in
addition to reactions only against another Meth's actions) so as to make
it absolutely clear that an action minion cannot use a reaction card,
well, then when the text of a card like Malk Mad Network breaks the first
tennant (only act when it's your turn) there is a loophole. The
potentially reacting vampires are still bound by the generic rule beacuse
the Network doesn't say anything about allowing them to react in their
Meth's turn.

We can only hope that the 'official' channels will come up with an
appropriate ruling on situations like these. And if they don't- well
you've heard my suggestion. Let's try and do it ourselves. Even if it's
not 'officially sanctioned' it gives players a reasonable set of
guidelines, and a forum for us to present our extensively playtested
critiques. The WoTC ought to be grateful for the input.

stephen

Messages.Author: Joseph Cochran
Messages.Body:
In article <3m0kec$m...@redwood.cs.scarolina.edu>,

L. Scott Johnson <sjoh...@math.scarolina.edu> wrote:

>>An easier ruling would be "Actions taken by a vamp using the madness network
>>count as part of their controller's turn".
>
>Well, that's fine for the Madness Network. What abou the expansion cards
>that end up with the same effect. A generic rule is always better than
>a specific one.

There is a perfectly fine general rule already in place.
Madness Network overrides (or at least should be fixed to override) the
rule. Any card that comes later should do the same. Fixing the generic
rules in a game with "The Golden Rule of Cards" should be done only very
rarely. The cards that break the rules are the ones that need to be
tuned and worded precisely. There is no reason to change the rules when
only one cards breaks the rule, there is plenty of reason to change the
card.
If we fix the rules for every card that breaks them, we'll never
work the kinks out.



>You're [L. Scott Johnson] changing the rules.

Scott is not changing the rules. He's re-writing the rules in a
form that more precisely specifies what it is intended to mean.

>See, I think that changing the rules of the game to accomodate
>the MN is more convoluted than changing the MN to fit the rules. That's
>the idea I'm advocating: fix the card.

The original rules, IMO, tried to state that reactions are only useable
on other's actions, and, involving the (not entirely correct) assumption
that actions are only performed on your own turn, got written in
the form that we see now. The source of the problem is not that the
Madness Network card breaks that assumption; it is in the rules
being ill-written in the first place, since it unnecessarily
involves an (incorrect) assumption. IMO, the rules of the game should be,
and was always intended to be, what Scott is stating now: action,
action modifiers and reactions played according to whose action it
is, not regarding to whose turn it is.

The fourth long article (coming soon!) of mine will clearly exploit an error
of your (Joseph's) proposed fix: you forgot to mention Out-of-Turn
Master cards in your proposed fix for the MMN.

>'Fraid I've gotta side with Joe on this one, now that I see his
>reasoning. The very reason that the Golden Rule of Cards is there is to
>deal with things that don't fall under the normal scope of the rules but
>are allowed by cards.

>Taking an action during someone else's turn certainly fits this category.

I'm not talking about fixing the rules for cards that break the rules.

I'm talking about fixing the rules for the cards that get broken by the
broken rules.

Obviously, if a card get broken by a good rule, then fix the card.
The golden rule is (for most people) a "good" rule - never in danger
of being fixed.

The rule of combat (combat does not occur if one of the minions is
in torpor) is a perfect example. Set the guidelines so people can know
how to play without looking up every card they play in the list of house
rules.

Reaction cards were meant to be used in response to actions. Let the rules
reflect that. (like they do if you remove the offending sentence in 7.2.2:
"These cards can only be played when it is not your turn." everything
works.) This is an example of fixing the logic in a game so that you don't
have to put bandages on the cards to accomplish the same thing.

If you don't agree that the rule is wrong (broken), then why not?
What possible reason could there be for restricting a Reaction card to
"not your turn" when it's already restricted to "other player's minion's
actions" ?

Reaction - a respons to an action.
How clear can it be?

L. Scott

The original rules stated that you can only take an action on
your turn. The logical opposite of that is that you can only react when
it's not your turn. The original rules are quite clear on the fact that
you can take actions only on your turn. Are you advocating changing
that part of the rules, too? Or will you agree that MN breaks that rule
as well?

>Madness Network card breaks that assumption; it is in the rules
>being ill-written in the first place, since it unnecessarily
>involves an (incorrect) assumption. IMO, the rules of the game should be,
>and was always intended to be, what Scott is stating now: action,
>action modifiers and reactions played according to whose action it
>is, not regarding to whose turn it is.

The MN breaks more rules than just the reaction rule, and is
thus proven to be a card that breaks the rules. The assumption that you
can only take actions on your turn is a basic tenant of the game, and MN
breaks that. It is therefore MN's responsibility to specify how it
should be handled.
You're conveniently forgetting the fact that MN breaks this
tenant when you say that the rules need rewriting. MN needs it because
it *consciously* breaks one of the basic rules of the game. If you
remove the assumption that you can only act on your turn, you break a
heckuva a lot more than the reaction rule. See?

>The fourth long article (coming soon!) of mine will clearly exploit an error
>of your (Joseph's) proposed fix: you forgot to mention Out-of-Turn
>Master cards in your proposed fix for the MMN.

No, I did not. I chose to leave it that way in my proposed
wording quite on purpose. However, it is trivial to add the wording to
fix the card for OOT's to my wording. It's still the MN that needs to
be fixed. I'm afraid that I'll probably disagree with this next one,
Alan.

>"not your turn" when it's already restricted to "other player's minion's

The rules are (greatly simplified): You take actions on your
turn. You use action modifiers on your actions. Other people react to
your actions. Thus they are only allowed to play reactions when it is
not their turn.
This is the chain of logic which defines the cardplay of the
game. This can be presented to the players in many ways. Any way that
does so effectively is fine. The way in the rulebook does so and is
fine. Maybe it should be changed in a revised edition of the game,
maybe not. However, it is not broken. The fundamental gameplay events
are perfectly defined.
The rule is not wrong because the rule defines normal gameplay
clearly, concisely, and understandably. The rule could be rewritten two
or three different ways, but that is how it was written, and that *does*
cover all aspects of normal gameplay, which is what the rules should do.
If a card wants to violate causality and change the basic assumptions of
the game, it's the card's responsibility to clean up the mess (by the
Golden Rule of Cards).
The *ONLY* card that breaks this chain of events is MN. And it
breaks it in a big way. The chain of logic is broken long before we
ever get to reactions. Suddenly you can take actions any time. The
card breaks the basic tenants of the game. It's not the rules' fault.
The rules are written to handle the game. It's the card's fault. The
card needs to clean up after itself.

A litmus test: if Madness Network didn't exist, would you have
any problems with the way the rules are written? Why?

My answer: no. It's patently obvious to me that you can only
take actions on your turn and only react on other people's turns (given
no MN).

Messages.Author: Stephen Beaulieu
Messages.Body:
I know I am about to open a can of worms that has been thoroughly
investigated and disagreed upon up till now. But as a good portion of the
discussion in the group focuses on the "Golden Rule of Cards", I thought I
would insert my thoughts on how that applies to cross table bleeds.

The rules as normally stated allow only a Meth to bleed her/his prey
only. This takes no cards, it just happens. You bleed your prey. In the
revised rules it furthermore states that a bleed is the fundamental
directed action taken by one vamp to undermine another Meth.
Also in the rules is the definition for the directed action symbol. This
defines the action as a directed action that only the Meth who is being
acted against can block. It also states that an action card with the D
symbol on it can be directed against any Meth.

Now here is where the "Golden Rule of Cards" applies. By creating bleed
action cards with the D symbol you allow bleeds against other Meths by
nature of the Golden Rule. The card overrules the normal rules. A bleed
is not normally allowed against anyone else but the acting Meths prey.
But the D symbol allows the action to be directed against any Meth, and
only that Meth can choose to block.

It seems very straightforward and logical to me. But, I am not everyone
else. I would be interested in hearing the opinions of the others on the
net, especially our honorable Elders. If it would please everyone else to
not hear the arguments for and against again, we could handle this
completely off net, through my email. I would prefer to have all the
discussions out in the open, so that everyone can contribute- but that
might create another huge thread, and I don't want to force people to read
what they might have already read before. I will state that I don't
expect to come to any sort of consensus about the ruling, but one can
always hope.

I should also state that this is how my group plays. We have _never_
yet had a problem with rampant cross table bleeding. When the bleeds
occur, it is usually for a valid reason (like taking awy the Edge from
someone who will win otherwise). I can think of maybe 5 times when a
cross table bleed has actually occurred.

Well, that's what I have to say on the matter. I am very interested in
the views of others.

Thanks in advance for understanding all the trouble I am causing.
stephen

Changing a generic rule has the advantage of applying to future cards, and
unanticipated side effects of existing cards. It has the disadvantage of
unanticipated side effects. As usual, it's a tradeoff.

error (a small error, but an error).

I have to disagree totally with this interpretation. Saying that Malks
can take actions out of turn, but not any that require action cards, is
like saying "Lucian can steal equipment as a strike, but he can't steal
a gun because the card doesn't specifically say gun." Come on. Some
actions require action cards. If Malkavians can perform actions out of
turn, they should be able to perform any action; if not, the card would
say "Malkavians can perform actions that do not require an action card"
or something to that effect.

Look at what 7.2.2 says about equipment cards; there's nothing to prevent
a Malkavian from equipping something out of turn because the rules don't
specifically say you can only use an equipment card on your own turn. It's
pretty clear that the rules say you can only play action cards on your
own turn because minions can't normally act out-of-turn, and that section
of the rules is trying to give an idea of the basic sequence of play.

It's not a big deal in any game I've been involved in, anyway. The only
actions Malks might want to do out of turn are things like Night Move,
Spying Mission, and maybe Govern the Unaligned, but I've never seen any
big advantage to doing these things out of turn (except possibly to to a
Night Move to get the Edge just before my turn starts). As a Malkavian
player, I'd much rather have a blood-gaining card like other clans have
(Art Museum, Arcane Library, Eco Terrorists) than the Madness Network.

Pat

>be played (since it wasn't the Malkavian's turn), which brought it back
>into line.

Actually, that was me who pointed it out. I had been aware of
the rules section for quite a while, but I was ignoring it in favor of
trying to promote a fix to the card, which has been and is still needed.
The reason I pointed it out when I did was because it shows how
silly it is to assume that the designer of the card actually wanted it
that way, when it's obvious that the effects of the card just weren't
thought out that far. It's a very Malkavian thing to be able to act out
of turn (game definition of turn :-)), it's a very rules-laywer thing to
say that you can and cannot play certain cards at certain times because
a card that is broken demands such by the letter of the law.



Messages.Author: Stephen Beaulieu
Messages.Body:
In article <3mmjss$k...@tribune.usask.ca>, sht...@herald.usask.ca (Shane
Hamish William Travis) wrote:

> I may be wrong here, but I don't think that anyone has a problem with
> Malkavians equipping using a MMN. Equipment cards are _equipment cards_,
> not action cards.

Well Shane I have to disagree with you here. In 12.3.1 under Equip Minions
an equipment card is described as an "action card...taht gives minions
special abilities." It is by this argument that we have decided that a
minion can only equip with 1 piece of equipment in a given action (as
opposed to taking an equip minion action and equipping with as much as the
Meth could pay for.)

So, according to 12.3.1, a Malk could _not_ equip using the Madness Network.

stephen

I'm not basing my guess (and I have never said that it is more
than my best guess) on your rulings alone. I'm basing it on several
months of watching the game, watching the newsgroup and the mailing
list, and on my experience with game design.
None of us can say what happened. All we can do is try to fix
the card as best as we can now. IMO, it needs it. In the DT's opinion,
the weird rule limitations are fine. I'll live with it. But I'll still
try to offer my best solution. The point here is to make the game the
best it can be. Despite the silence from the rules team on many things,
I believe that they have the best interests of the game at heart, too.
